title: Latency slicing & fused-op coalescence labbook
content:
Purpose
This is a working labbook for a set of targeted experiments exploring how "latency slicing" (deliberately subdividing requests and scheduling smaller slices) interacts with fused-operator coalescence in the attention hot path. Goal: find practical knobs that reduce 95/99th token latency for tail-heavy workloads without regressing median or throughput by >5%.

Background/context
We have recurring customer reports of token-level micro-latency spikes (~10–40 ms) for mid-length sequences (L=512–1024) on multi-tenant Dedicated clusters. Prior investigations pointed at (a) kernel launch / queuing jitter when many small concurrent requests hit the GPU, (b) occasional KV-cache contention when slices overlap, and (c) suboptimal fusion choices that force additional global synchronizations. Existing notes captured elsewhere (see linked artifacts) focus on profiling FlashAttention and paged-attention variants individually; this labbook is about their interaction with our scheduler and the fused-op coalescer (the runtime pass that merges adjacent elementwise + softmax + matmul kernels).

Hypotheses
1) Creating smaller, aligned "slices" for long sequences and scheduling them with bounded concurrency reduces tail latency by smoothing queuing bursts, but increases total kernel launches and could worsen median latency.
2) The fused-op coalescer currently merges operations conservatively; more aggressive coalescing reduces DRAM traffic and kernel-launch overhead, but may increase register pressure and cause occasional kernel retries on memory-limited GPUs.
3) FlashAttention-v2-like kernels that assume contiguous KV layouts perform worse when slices are noncontiguous (paged attention). Adding a lightweight defragmentation step or rebase buffer can restore kernel efficiency with small overhead.

Testbed
- Hardware: NVIDIA A10g (primary), p4d-8x (secondary), RTX6000 for dev reproductions.
- Runtime: local dev build of serving-runtime branch latency-slice-experiment (commit: 3f7c1a2).
- Models: llama-13b distilled config, sequence lengths 256/512/1024.
- Kernel variants: flash-v1 (baseline), flash-v2-tiling, paged-attn (page-size 64/128), fused-coalesce (conservative), fused-coalesce-aggressive.
- Workloads: 1) steady 200 rps tiny (payloads with short seq), 2) mixed tails (80% short, 20% long), 3) tail-bursty (periodic spikes of concurrent long seq)

Measurement methodology
- Use local tracer and NVTX markers in serving runtime to capture per-token token-latency (arrival->emit).
- Collect GPU-side traces with nvprof/Nsight where possible and use per-kernel durations.
- Measure p50/p90/p95/p99 of token latency and end-to-end request latency. Also report tokens/sec and GPU utilization.
- Each experiment run: 10k tokens warmup, 60k tokens steady, repeated 3 times.

Commands & scripts
- run harness: ./tools/load_test --scenario mixed-tails --model llama13b --kernel flash-v2-tiling --slices 4 --concurrency-limit 16 --out run-mixed-flashv2.json
- collect nvtx: export RUNTIME_NVTX=1; ./bin/serve --config cfg.json & sleep 5; ./tools/nvprof_collect.sh pid
- quick microbench: python tools/kernel_probe.py --model llama13b --kernel fused-coalesce-aggressive --seq 512 --batch 1 --reps 1000

Preliminary results (summary)
- Baseline (flash-v1, no-slicing, conservative-fuse): p95 token latency ~ 48ms, p99 ~ 82ms on A10g, median ~ 18ms. GPU util ~72%.
- Slicing=4 + conservative-fuse: p95 down to 36ms, p99 down to 63ms, median increases slightly to 20ms; tokens/sec -3%. Observed fewer large queuing spikes in host-side queue depth plots.
- Slicing=4 + aggressive-fuse: p95 30ms, p99 55ms, median 22ms; tokens/sec -6% (some throughput loss). GPU registers and shared memory utilization higher by ~12% in Nsight snapshots.
- Paged-attn (page=64) without rebase buffer + slicing: flash-v2 kernels show 10–18% slower per-kernel times relative to contiguous case; p99 regresses by ~15ms.
- Paged-attn + small defrag rebase (copy into contiguous staging buffer for slice): overhead ~2–4ms per token but restores kernel throughput; net p99 wins when slice size > 3 pages.

Notable traces and artifacts
- NVTX trace: nvtx-run-2025-08-20-2.json — shows host-queue spikes at t=120s correlating with p99 spikes.
- Nsight capture: nsight-burst-aug21 captures register-pressure during fused-aggressive kernels where kernel runtime has variable stalls.
- Kernel-probe outputs: kernel-probe-512x1-fused-aggr.csv — shows tail latency of matmul-softmax fusion rising when free blocks < threshold.

Detailed observations (by experiment)
1) Slicing-only (no-coalesce change)
- Host scheduler becomes smoother: instead of dispatching one huge kernel for a long seq, we dispatch 4 smaller kernels which occupy the GPU in overlapping but staggered fashion. This reduced queueing jitter but increased kernel launch counts. The runtime's kernel-launch batching path has a ~0.6ms amortized cost per kernel; at slice counts >8 we start to lose median throughput.
- KV-cache hits: slices that overlap same KV ranges introduced contention in the KV cache mutex in our runtime; adding per-shard reader-writer lock reduced contention.

2) Fused-op aggressive coalescing
- Aggressive merging achieves fewer global kernels (reduce launches by ~35%), less global mem traffic, and improved L2 reuse. However, it increases register pressure and sometimes triggers fallback to a non-fused path on low-memory devices. We observed several 'fallback-to-slow' incidents on p4d when slice concurrency spikes.
- In some cases (batch=1, seq=512) aggressive fusion reduced p95 by 40% but p99 still depends on host scheduling jitter. So fusion cannot fully mask queueing issues.

3) Paged-attention interactions
- Paged attention with small page sizes breaks assumptions in flash-v2 kernels that expect contiguous KV. Two mitigation strategies: (a) rebase copy for slice into small contiguous staging buffer; (b) change kernel to accept strided access (costly). We prototyped (a) and it worked well when slice sizes amortized the copy cost.

Quick recommendations (temporary)
- Default runtime: enable slicing=4 for sequences >512 with concurrency limit set to 12 for Dedicated clusters with >1 tenant. This showed consistent p99 reductions without >5% throughput loss in our sample hardware.
- Keep conservative fuse as default; enable aggressive-fuse behind a runtime flag and telemetry that records fallback events. Only enable aggressive on single-tenant Dedicated where memory pressure is known.
- Implement lightweight rebase buffer for paged-attn slices: copy into contiguous staging if slice > 3 pages or if kernel reports strided penalty.

Action items
- [Priya] Add telemetry counters for kernel-fallback reasons (register-pressure / OOM / launch-timeout) — JIRA: RI-4520 (due 2025-09-10).
- [Evan] Prototype rebase staging buffer as an opt-in runtime pass and measure copy overheads (CI microbench + A10g run).
- [Marco] Add scheduler knob to dynamically adjust slice count based on recent queue depth percentiles; roll experiment in canary.
- [Aisha] Update docs for Dedicated tuning guide with new default slicing suggestion and diagnostics to watch (nvtx markers, kernel-fallback counts).

Open questions / risks
- Does aggressive fusion cause silent correctness issues for weird model configs (rmsnorm fused differently)? Need unit-test matrix across model ops.
- Multi-GPU/multi-instance scenarios: how does cross-instance packing interact with slicing? Could cause cross-tenant interference if not isolated.
- Cost model: small slices increase host CPU & PCIe copy overhead — quantify across instance types (A10g vs p4d).

Appendix: small data table (representative single-run numbers, A10g, mixed-tails)
- baseline: p50 18ms, p95 48ms, p99 82ms, tokens/sec 12.2k
- slice4 + cons-fuse: p50 20ms, p95 36ms, p99 63ms, tokens/sec 11.9k
- slice4 + aggr-fuse: p50 22ms, p95 30ms, p99 55ms, tokens/sec 11.5k
- paged(64)+slice4 no-rebase: p50 25ms, p95 44ms, p99 70ms, tokens/sec 10.8k
- paged(64)+slice4 + rebase: p50 23ms, p95 37ms, p99 58ms, tokens/sec 11.1k

Notes to self
- Capture larger nsight for p4d if time allows; look specifically at L2 traffic heatmaps and shared-mem bank conflicts.
- Cross-reference with "kernel-latency-variance-decomposition-notes" (existing doc) to map variance sources.

End of labbook entry (draft).
